title: Angels Bound, Giants Slain, the World Drowned
sum: The angels of the Lord, sent to the earth in 4:15, take human wives, and their children are giants. Violence spreads to every creature, and God resolves to wipe out all flesh except Noah. The angels of the presence bind the guilty angels in the depths of the earth, while the giants are handed the sword and kill one another as their fathers watch.

The angel then pauses the story for a short sermon: every judgment is written on the heavenly tablets, the judge takes no bribes, and Israel will be forgiven if it turns, "once a year." The Flood follows Genesis closely, but with exact dates on every step, seven windows of the sky, the ark resting on Mount Lubar, and dates that fit a year of 364 days.
readings: Read as an answer to Genesis 6:1-4

Genesis tells of the sons of God and the Nephilim in four puzzling verses and never says what became of them. Jubilees answers: they were angels; their sons were giants; the angels were bound and the giants destroyed one another before the Flood.
Read as a sermon on judgment

Verses 13-18 turn the Flood into a lesson for Israel. What happened to the world then shows that every sin is written down, and that God keeps a way back open for Israel through repentance and the Day of Atonement.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church counts Kufale as Scripture, so for its readers this chapter belongs to the Bible, alongside 1 Enoch, which the same church also counts as Scripture.
views.H: Historical critics see the writer combining Genesis 6-8 with the Watchers story of 1 Enoch 6-16, but softening it: the angels came down to do good (4:15) and fell only here. Charles thought verses 10-16 were first written about the final judgment and later bent to the past.
views.N: Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 speak of angels kept in chains for judgment; 1 Peter 3:19-20 of spirits who disobeyed in Noah's day. Jubilees, like 1 Enoch, shows that these ideas were current among Jews before the New Testament was written.
views.J: Jubilees reads the sons of God as angels, as 1 Enoch does. Charles calls this "the older Jewish view," which, he says, "was condemned probably as early as the first cent. A.D." He compares Jubilees' teaching on the Day of Atonement (5:17-18) with the Mishnah, which says the Day does not atone for one who sins planning to repent.
views.W: Churches that do not count Jubilees as Scripture can still read the chapter as an ancient Jewish interpretation of Genesis 6, useful background for Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4.

deep.h: Binding and slaughter: one story told twice
deep.b:
Jubilees tells the Watchers' fate in the order of 1 Enoch 10: the angels are bound "in the depths of the earth" (5:6, 10), and their sons are sent against one another with the sword (5:7, 9), while the fathers watch (5:10; 1 Enoch 10:12). Only then does the Flood come. So the giants do not drown; the Flood is for the rest of corrupted creation. Jubilees adds that the binding was done by the narrators themselves, the angels of the presence (5:6).

What happens to the giants' spirits is not told here. Chapter 10 picks it up: the spirits of the giants become the demons that trouble Noah's grandsons (10:5).

Verses 13-18 interrupt the story. The angel tells Moses that the judgment of every creature is written on the heavenly tablets, that God shows no favoritism and takes no bribes (Deuteronomy 10:17), and that "about the children of Israel" a different decree stands: if they turn, he forgives. The final line, "once a year," ties that forgiveness to the Day of Atonement. Charles noted that Jubilees here demands real turning from sin, not the ritual alone, and saw it standing between Leviticus 16 and later rabbinic teaching.

echoes: Genesis 6:1-8:19; 1 Enoch 6:1-10:16; Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4-5; 1 Peter 3:19-20; Leviticus 16:29-34; Hebrews 9:7; Deuteronomy 10:17

settings.when: in the middle of the story of the Flood
settings.why: To turn the Flood into a warning and a hope: every sin is recorded and judged, yet Israel has a way back by turning to God, renewed each year on the Day of Atonement.
settings.readers: Who wrote the book, and when, is debated. Charles (1902) held that it "was written in Hebrew by a Pharisee" between 135 and 105 BC, under the high priest John Hyrcanus. Grintz (Encyclopaedia Judaica) holds that "the author was not a Pharisee" and places him at the end of Hyrcanus' reign. For its first readers the sermon ties forgiveness to turning from sin "once a year," the Day of Atonement, a point Charles compares with the Mishnah.

settings.what: God's decree on the giants' days
settings.to: no hearer named; reported by the angel
settings.when: as the order goes out to destroy the giants
settings.why: In Genesis 6:3 the 120 years seem to limit human life or set a time before the Flood. Placed here, between the order and the sword, the words read as a limit on the giants.
settings.readers: Readers who knew Genesis 6:3 would meet its words in a new place, between the order to destroy the giants and the sword sent among them.

title: The Covenant, the Feast of Weeks and the Year of 364 Days
sum: Noah leaves the ark on the first day of the third month, makes atonement for the earth and offers a full priestly sacrifice. God makes a covenant with him: no more flood, the seasons will not fail, all food is given but blood is forbidden, and whoever spills human blood will die. Noah and his sons swear to it. The angel tells Moses that this is why Israel swore a covenant with blood in the same month at Sinai.

The covenant is renewed every year at the Feast of Weeks, a feast kept in heaven since creation, by Noah, and by Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, then forgotten until Sinai. The chapter ends with the book's calendar law: four quarter days, thirteen weeks to a quarter, a year of exactly 364 days, and a warning that watching the moon will ruin the feasts.
readings: Read as covenant history
One covenant runs from Noah through Abraham to Sinai, all made in the third month and renewed each year at the Feast of Weeks. Sinai does not begin something new; it restores what the world had lost.
Read as a calendar argument
The chapter is the heart of Jubilees' case for a 364-day year. By writing the calendar into the Flood itself, the writer makes it as old as the covenant and as binding as the ban on blood.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church counts Kufale as Scripture, so for its readers the covenant with Noah, the blood law and the calendar of this chapter are Scripture.
views.H: Critical scholars see here the writer's central causes: a covenant renewed at the Feast of Weeks, the ban on blood, and above all a 364-day year set against calendars that follow the moon. Charles thought the writers chose 364 days so that every feast would fall on the same weekday each year.
views.N: The Feast of Weeks is Pentecost, when the Spirit came (Acts 2:1). The blood ban appears in the apostles' letter to Gentile believers (Acts 15:20, 29). Paul warns the Galatians who were "keeping close track of days, months, seasons and years" (Galatians 4:10), and Colossians 2:16 lets no one judge believers over "a festival, a new moon or Sabbaths."
views.J: Grintz (Encyclopaedia Judaica) notes that the Beta Israel of Ethiopia based their calendar, especially the date of Shavuot, on Jubilees. He also notes that the book, like the rabbis' halakhah, knows four "new years," and that it fixes Shavuot so that it always falls on a Sunday, a way of reading "from the day after the Sabbath" (Leviticus 23:15) with which, Grintz says, the Pharisees disagreed. Charles notes that later Judaism (Maimonides) held the Feast of Weeks to celebrate the giving of the law on Sinai.
views.W: Churches that do not count Jubilees as Scripture read the chapter as a witness to Jewish debates about the calendar before Christ. They do not keep its 364-day year. See the card at 1 Enoch 82 on keeping a set calendar.

deep.b:
Jubilees' own verses fix the shape of the year: four quarters of thirteen weeks (6:29), opened by the first days of months 1, 4, 7 and 10, the "days of remembrance" (6:23), in all fifty-two weeks (6:30) and "364 days" (6:32). They do not say how long each month is, and readers fill that in differently. Grintz (Encyclopaedia Judaica) describes months of 30 days each except the third, sixth, ninth and twelfth, which have 31. Charles (1902) read the year as twelve months with "4 intercalary days," rejected Frankel's view of thirteen months of 28 days, and reported Eppstein's view that Jubilees used two years at once: a civil year of twelve months (eight of 30 days and four of 31) and a year for the feasts of thirteen months of 28 days.

Because 364 divides by seven, every date falls on the same weekday every year. Charles thought this was the point: the writers knew Greek calendars and still chose 364 days, out of "dogmatic prejudice," so that each feast would always fall on the same day of the week. A true solar year is about 365 and a quarter days. He also reported B. W. Bacon's argument that the Flood dates of Genesis already assume a year ten days longer than the moon's 354, the "ten days" of 6:36.

Genesis 1:14 says the lights in the sky "will be signs, and will mark the appointed times, the days and the years," and Psalm 104:19 says, "He made the moon to keep the appointed times." Jubilees reads the matter differently: the sun alone rules the year (2:9), and those who follow the moon will make "a despised day" of a holy one (6:37). This is one place where Jubilees conflicts with the plain sense of the 66 books.

1 Enoch's Astronomical Book (chapters 72-82) teaches the same total: "The year comes to exactly 364 days" (1 Enoch 72:32), and "The year is complete in 364 days" (1 Enoch 82:6). But it also describes the moon at length (1 Enoch 73-74) and says, "The moon brings in the years for them exactly" (1 Enoch 74:12). Charles (1902) wrote that Jubilees "seems to be a polemic against the teaching of Ethiopic Enoch lxxiii.-lxxiv." That is his theory, and it is narrow: the two books share the 364-day year and differ only on whether the moon has any part in the count. He adds that the Samaritan Chronicle, which knew Jubilees, rejected it and held, from Genesis 1:14, that the year must be reckoned by both sun and moon. Grintz says the solar calendar was "already familiar from the Book of Enoch and the Dead Sea Scrolls." For how churches answer the question, see the card at 1 Enoch 82, "Must God's people keep a set calendar of holy days?"

deep.h: The Feast of Weeks as covenant renewal
deep.b: In Leviticus 23:15-21 and Deuteronomy 16:9-12 the Feast of Weeks is a harvest feast. Jubilees keeps that side, "the Feast of Firstfruits," but adds a second: the feast is the yearly renewal of the covenant with Noah (6:17), kept by Abraham (15:1-2) and restored at Sinai (6:19). Grintz notes that in Jubilees Shavuot commemorates "the renewal of the covenant" after the Flood. Charles notes that later Judaism (Maimonides) held the feast to celebrate the giving of the law on Sinai; Jubilees already ties it to the covenant made in the same month at Sinai (6:11).

deep.title: Claude's theory: why the calendar sits in the Flood story
deep.b: Jubilees could have given its calendar law at creation (chapter 2) or at the Exodus. It gives it here. One reason may be that the Flood is the one story in Genesis dated day by day (Genesis 7:11; 8:4-5, 13-14). By tying each quarter day to a moment of the Flood (6:25-27), the writer makes his calendar look as if it had been read out of Genesis itself, not brought into it. Charles reports a similar argument by Bacon about the dates of Genesis; the link with the placing of the law in chapter 6 is Claude's.

echoes: Genesis 8:20-9:17; Exodus 19:1; Exodus 24:3-8; Exodus 34:22; Leviticus 17:10-14; Leviticus 23:15-21; Numbers 28:26-31; 1 Enoch 72:32; 1 Enoch 74:12; 1 Enoch 82:4-6; Acts 2:1; Acts 15:20; Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16

settings.to: Noah and his sons, on Mount Lubar after the Flood
settings.when: after Noah's sacrifice on the first day of the third month
settings.why: To promise a stable world, give all food but forbid blood, and protect human life because humans bear God's image.
settings.readers: In the book's own frame the laws on blood and murder are given to Noah, so they bind all humankind, not only Israel; Charles's notes trace each one to Genesis 9:1-7.

settings.what: The law of blood and the oath of the covenant
settings.when: as Moses receives the law in the third month
settings.why: To show Moses that the blood rite of Exodus 24 renews Noah's covenant, and to bind Israel to the ban on eating blood forever, with priests pleading for Israel at the altar morning and evening.
settings.readers: Charles (1902) ties the offerings "morning and evening" of 6:14 to the daily offering of Numbers 28:3-8: readers who knew the Temple's daily sacrifice heard it presented as part of Noah's covenant.

settings.what: The law of the Feast of Weeks
settings.to: Moses, for the children of Israel
settings.when: on Sinai, in the month of the feast
settings.why: To fix the feast once a year, in the third month, as both a harvest feast and the renewal of the covenant, and to trace it from heaven through Noah and the patriarchs.
settings.readers: Grintz notes that the Beta Israel of Ethiopia based their calendar and the date of Shavuot on Jubilees: here the passage shaped a living community's practice.

settings.when: on Sinai, after the law of the Feast of Weeks
settings.why: To command a year of exactly 364 days and warn that a moon-based count will put holy days on the wrong dates and lead Israel into the nations' feasts.
settings.readers: Grintz (Encyclopaedia Judaica) says the solar calendar this law commands was "already familiar from the Book of Enoch and the Dead Sea Scrolls," and that the Beta Israel of Ethiopia later based their calendar on Jubilees. So the law was read by Jews who argued for a year not set by the moon; Charles saw the Samaritan Chronicle answering it from the other side.

title: Noah's Vineyard and Noah's Last Charge
sum: Noah plants vines on Mount Lubar, waits for the fourth-year fruit, and opens the wine at a New Year feast with a full sacrifice. He becomes drunk and lies uncovered; Ham sees and tells, Shem and Japheth cover him. Noah curses Canaan and blesses Shem and Japheth. Ham leaves his father in anger, Japheth follows out of jealousy, and each builds a city named for his wife, while Shem stays beside Noah.

In the twenty-eighth jubilee Noah gives his grandsons a charge: do right, cover your nakedness, bless the Creator, honor parents, love one another, and keep away from sexual sin. The Flood came, he says, because of the Watchers' sin and the giants' bloodshed. He forbids murder and eating blood, orders blood covered with earth, and teaches the law of fruit trees, handed down from Enoch.
readings: Read as a family story
Genesis 9:20-27 is a brief, troubling story. Jubilees tells it as the start of the brothers' rivalry, which grows into the quarrel over land in chapters 8-10.
Read as a law code before Sinai

Noah's charge (7:20-39) gives the nations a short law: justice, modesty, worship, honor of parents, love of neighbor, sexual purity, no murder, no blood. Jubilees shows that God's basic laws were known long before Moses.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church counts Kufale as Scripture, so Noah's commands here stand in its Bible beside the laws of the books of Moses.
views.H: Critical scholars see the writer giving Noah laws that Leviticus gives to Israel: the fourth-year fruit (Leviticus 19:23-25), covering blood (Leviticus 17:13), the death of the murderer (Numbers 35:33). Charles thought 7:20-39 came from an older Book of Noah, since Noah speaks in the first person from 7:26.
views.N: Charles thought 2 Peter 2:5, which calls Noah "a herald of righteousness," knew this speech. The apostles' letter of Acts 15:20, 29 asks Gentile believers to avoid sexual sin and blood, two of Noah's commands here.
views.J: Charles compares the "three things" of 7:21 with Genesis Rabbah 31, which names idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed as the causes of the Flood, and with the Talmud's three sins one must die rather than commit (Sanhedrin 74a).
views.W: Churches that do not count Jubilees as Scripture read the chapter as a witness to how Jews before Christ thought the nations should live.

deep.b:
Noah's charge has three parts. First, general duties: do what is right, cover nakedness, bless the Creator, honor father and mother, love one another, and avoid sexual sin and uncleanness (7:20). Second, blood: no murder, no eating blood, and cover the blood of animals killed (7:27-33). Third, the law of fruit trees (7:35-37). Each part is tied to the Flood: the world was destroyed for sexual sin and bloodshed (7:21-25), and Noah fears his grandsons are starting down the same road (7:26-27).

Charles noted that the writer credits laws to Enoch (7:38-39), so the chain of teaching runs Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah. Jubilees will extend it through Shem (10:14) to Levi (45:16).

echoes: Genesis 9:18-29; Genesis 10:1-7, 22; Leviticus 17:10-14; Leviticus 19:23-25; Numbers 35:33; 1 Enoch 7:1-6; 2 Peter 2:5; Jude 14; Acts 15:20

settings.what: Noah's curse on Canaan and blessing of Shem and Japheth
settings.when: the morning after the New Year feast on Mount Lubar
settings.why: To curse Canaan, Ham's youngest son, for his father's act, and to bless Shem as the line in whose dwelling the Lord will live.
settings.readers: Charles (1902) thought the book's account of the lots (8:10-10:34) answered objections, current in the second century BC, to Israel's taking of Canaan. The curse on Canaan here prepares that claim.

settings.when: in the twenty-eighth jubilee, as his family begins to split and quarrel
settings.why: To warn them that the sins that brought the Flood (sexual sin, uncleanness and bloodshed) are already among them, and to hand on the laws he received from his fathers.
settings.readers: Charles (1902) thought the speech came from an older Book of Noah that the writer took over, since Noah speaks in the first person from 7:26. Its laws on blood and fruit trees (7:28-37) are laws Leviticus gives to Israel, here put in Noah's mouth for all his descendants.

title: Kainam's Stone and the Lots of the Earth
sum: Arpachshad's son Kainam, a name found in the Greek Genesis and in Luke 3:36 but not in the Hebrew, finds the Watchers' star-lore carved on a rock, copies it and goes astray. The line goes on through Shelah and Eber to Peleg, named because the earth was divided in his days.

Noah's descendants first divide the earth wrongly. Then, with an angel present, Noah has his three sons draw lots from his robe. Shem's lot is the middle of the earth, with Eden, Sinai and Zion, "facing one another"; Ham's is the hot south beyond the Gihon; Japheth's is the cold north beyond the Tina. Noah rejoices, remembering his blessing of Shem.
readings: Read as sacred geography

The map puts Israel's land at the center of the world, with the three holy places of creation, law and kingship in it. Charles identified the rivers with the Don and the Nile, so the map follows Greek geography of the writer's day.
Read as a legal deed
The lots are a title deed to the land, drawn before God's angel. Whoever later settles outside his lot breaks a sworn agreement (9:14-15; 10:29-34).

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church counts Kufale as Scripture, so this division of the earth stands in its Bible. In it the Gihon, the river of Eden that circles "the whole land of Cush" (Genesis 2:13), is the boundary of Ham's portion.
views.H: Charles identified the map's names with those of Greek geography (the Tina with the Don, Rafa with the Rhipaean mountains, Me'at with the Sea of Azov) and saw the main aim of the division in 10:29-34: to answer objections to Israel's taking of Canaan by showing that the land was Shem's by lot.
views.N: Luke 3:36 lists "the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad," the same extra generation as 8:1. Acts 17:26 says God "fixed their set seasons and the limits of the places where they would live"; Jubilees tells one version of how.
views.J: Charles notes that the rabbis also called the land of Israel the navel of the world, with Jerusalem in its center. Later midrash, such as Pirke de-Rabbi Eliezer 24, also tells of the division of the earth.
views.W: Churches that do not count Jubilees as Scripture read the chapter as an ancient Jewish map of the world. Its Kainam (8:1) is the same extra generation found in the Greek Genesis and in Luke 3:36.

deep.b:
The boundaries are hard to follow, and Charles admitted that much is unclear. In outline: Shem's lot is the middle band of the earth, from the Tina (the Don, Charles thought) east to the Garden of Eden and south to the Gihon (the Nile). Ham's lot is everything south and west of the Gihon, as far as the sea of Atel (the Atlantic) and Gadir (Cadiz). Japheth's lot is the cold north, from Gog in the east to Gadir in the west, with five great islands. Shem's land alone is "neither hot nor cold" (8:30).

Charles compared Epiphanius and Syncellus, Christian writers who drew on Jubilees and gave Shem the lands "from Persia and Bactria as far as India" and "as far as Rhinocorura," on the border of Egypt.

Noah "knew that the Garden of Eden is the Holy of Holies and the dwelling of the Lord, Mount Sinai the center of the desert, and Mount Zion the center of the navel of the earth" (8:19). The three places mark creation, the law and the Temple. All three lie in Shem's portion, so God's dwelling, promised in Noah's blessing (7:12), is in Shem's land.

echoes: Genesis 10:1-32; Genesis 11:10-17; Luke 3:36; Ezekiel 38:12; Ezekiel 5:5; Deuteronomy 32:8; Acts 17:26; Genesis 2:8-14

settings.what: The division of the earth by lot, and the oath
settings.by: Noah, with one of the angels of the presence present
settings.to: his three sons and their children
settings.when: at the beginning of the thirty-third jubilee
settings.why: To give each son a fixed portion by God's lot, and to bind every descendant by oath and curse never to take another's land.
settings.readers: Charles thought the passage answered objections, current in the writer's day, to Israel's conquest of Canaan: the land had been Shem's by lot all along.

title: Sixteen Grandsons, Sixteen Portions
sum: Each son of Noah divides his land among his own sons. Ham's four sons get bands running west from Cush to Canaan by the sea. Shem's five sons get Elam toward India, Asshur with Nineveh and Shinar, Arpachshad with the Chaldeans and Lebanon, Aram with Mesopotamia, and Lud the mountains toward the Great Sea. Japheth's seven sons get the north, the islands and the "tongues" of land in the west.

Noah then makes them all swear an oath under a curse: no one may take a portion that did not fall to him by lot. They answer, "So be it! So be it!" for themselves and their children until the day of judgment.
readings: Read as a map of the nations
Jubilees turns the names of Genesis 10 into places on a map, so the reader can see where every nation belongs.
Read as the setup for Canaan's crime
The oath of 9:14-15 is the law that Canaan breaks in 10:29-34. The chapter prepares a court case.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church counts Kufale as Scripture, so this account of how the nations of Genesis 10 received their lands stands in its Bible.
views.H: The map reflects the writer's own world: the sons of Javan, the Greeks, hold only islands and coasts. Charles took Canaan's lot to be north-west Africa, far from the land of Israel, and Madai's to take in Britain and Ireland.
views.N: Paul says God "made every nation of humankind out of one person" and fixed "the limits of the places where they would live" (Acts 17:26). Jubilees is an older Jewish example of the same belief.
views.J: Charles points to Josephus (Antiquities 1.6) and the medieval Chronicles of Jerahmeel, which also place each grandson of Noah in a land.
views.W: Churches that do not count Jubilees as Scripture read the chapter as ancient geography and as background to Genesis 10.

title: Mastema's Tenth, Noah's Book, and the Tower
sum: Unclean demons, the spirits of the Watchers' sons, lead Noah's grandsons astray, blind them and kill them. Noah prays, and God orders the angels to bind them all. But Mastema, chief of the spirits, asks that some be left to him, since human evil is great; God leaves him a tenth and sends nine parts to the place of judgment. An angel teaches Noah the cures for the spirits' diseases with plants, Noah writes them in a book, and he gives all his books to Shem. Noah dies at 950 years.

Peleg's son Reu is named for the evil plan of Shinar. The builders bake bricks for forty-three years to climb into heaven; the Lord and his angels come down, mix up their languages, and a wind throws the tower down. Then Canaan, seeing the good land "from Lebanon to the Brook of Egypt," refuses to go to his own lot and settles in Shem's, under the curse he swore to. Madai, by contrast, asks for land in Media and receives it.
readings: Read as a story about evil spirits
Chapter 10 explains why evil spirits still trouble the world after the Flood: God allowed a tenth to stay, under Mastema, to test and punish human sin, and gave Noah remedies against them.
Read as a story about land
The second half explains why the land of Israel was called Canaan, and claims that Canaan took it unlawfully, against an oath sworn before God's angel.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church counts Kufale as Scripture, so Mastema, the tenth of the spirits left to him and Noah's book of healing stand in its Bible.
views.H: Read historically, the chapter gives a Jewish account of evil: demons are the giants' spirits (as in 1 Enoch 15-16), but they act only by God's permission, under a leader who plays the Satan's part of Job 1-2. Charles thought 10:1-14 came from a Book of Noah, and saw the Canaan story as an answer to objections against the conquest.
views.N: The Gospels speak of "the ruler of the demons" (Mark 3:22) and of demons who fear the Abyss (Luke 8:31). Here a chief of the spirits rules a remnant of demons by God's leave, an idea close to the Gospels' world.
views.J: Charles reports that the medieval Hebrew Book of Noah keeps parts of 10:1-2 and 9-14 and names the healing angel Raphael. The Babel story is close to Genesis 11, with details (the wind, the size of the tower) found also in later Jewish and Christian writers.
views.W: Churches that do not count Jubilees as Scripture do not take Mastema or the tenth of the spirits as doctrine. For the church debate on where demons come from, see the card at 1 Enoch 15.

deep.h: Mastema and the tenth of the spirits
deep.b:
Mastema appears for the first time in 10:8 as "the chief of the spirits." He asks God, as the Satan does in Job 1:9-12, to leave him some of the spirits, since "the evil of humankind is great." God grants a tenth; nine parts go down to the place of judgment (10:9), and the angels leave the rest "to serve before Satan on the earth" (10:11). So in Jubilees the leader of the spirits is the Satan, but he acts only within limits God sets.

Charles reports Syncellus's Greek summary: "the devil asked to take a portion of them for the testing of men," and the tenth was given "so as to tempt men for the testing of each one's choice toward God." He also explains the name from Hebrew: masṭemah, "hostility" (Hosea 9:7-8), from the same root as satan. Mastema returns in Jubilees as "Prince Mastema," who proposes Abraham's test (17:16) and opposes Moses (48:2, 9).

Canaan's lot was in the far west of Ham's portion (9:1). Instead he settles "in the land of Lebanon," from Hamath to the entrance of Egypt, the very borders of Israel (10:29, 33). His father and brothers warn him that he is breaking the oath sworn before "the holy judge" and will be cursed (10:30-32). He refuses, and the land is named after him (10:34).

Charles thought the story answers a moral objection to Israel's conquest of Canaan, an objection he believed was current in the writer's time: Israel did not seize another people's land, it took back its own. He quotes Epiphanius and Syncellus making the same argument. Genesis gives a different reason for the conquest: "the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full" (Genesis 15:16), and Leviticus 18:24-28 says the land vomited out its people for their sins. The two explanations stand side by side: one rests on a sworn deed, the other on judgment for wrongdoing.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a tithe of evil
deep.b: Jubilees cares about tithes, and here God keeps nine parts of the spirits and leaves one part, a tenth, to Mastema. The reversal may be deliberate: evil is given a measured "tithe" of the spirits, a fixed portion that it may not exceed. This reading is Claude's; Charles and the Greek summary in Syncellus speak only of "the tenth."

echoes: Genesis 9:28-29; Genesis 11:1-9; Genesis 10:15-20; Genesis 15:16; Job 1:6-12; Numbers 16:22; Mark 3:22; Luke 8:31; 1 Enoch 15:8-12; Tobit 12:14-15

settings.what: Noah's prayer against the evil spirits
settings.when: after his sons tell him the demons are killing his grandsons
settings.why: To ask God, who saved him from the Flood, to imprison the spirits and keep them from ruling over the righteous.
settings.readers: Charles (1902) reports that fragments of 10:1-2 and 10:9-14 survive in the medieval Hebrew Book of Noah, which names the healing angel Raphael: later Jewish readers kept this account of the spirits and of Noah's remedies.

settings.to: the Lord; then the angels of the presence
settings.when: as the angels begin to bind the spirits
settings.why: To explain why evil spirits remain after God's judgment: by God's permission, a tenth are left to test and punish human sin.
settings.readers: Charles reports that the Greek chronicler Syncellus summarized the scene for Christian readers as "the testing of each one's choice toward God."

settings.when: as the tower rises in Shinar
settings.why: To announce the mixing of languages and the scattering of the peoples until the day of judgment.
settings.readers: In the book's own frame the angels say "we came down with him" (10:23), so the "us" of Genesis 11:7 is God with his angels.

settings.what: Ham, Cush and Mizraim warn Canaan
settings.when: after Canaan settles in the land of Lebanon
settings.why: To warn him that he is in a land not his by lot and under the curse sworn before the holy judge.
settings.readers: Charles thought the scene answered objections to the conquest of Canaan in the writer's own day.
